content: This document provides interim guidance for countries on laboratory testing strategies and considerations for severe acute hepatitis of unknown cause in children. It outlines diagnostic approaches grouped into three categories: (1) tests required to meet the current WHO case definition, (2) additional diagnostics to exclude other recognized causes of severe acute hepatitis in children, and (3) investigative diagnostics to identify potential causes. Early collection of key specimens, such as whole blood, serum, plasma, throat swabs, stool, or urine, is strongly encouraged, with whole blood being the preferred specimen type. Liver biopsies should only be performed if clinically necessary. Consultation with a pediatric hepatologist is recommended for these assessments. Investigative diagnostics may include testing for a wide range of viruses, bacteria, parasites, and fungi, with adaptations based on the country or region's endemic diseases. If local laboratory capacity is limited, referral to regional or global laboratories is advised, and positive specimens should be stored for further testing or investigation. Cases of severe acute hepatitis of unknown cause in children have been reported across multiple countries, with most cases originating from the WHO European Region. Probable cases and those pending classification have also been reported in the Americas, Western Pacific, South-East Asia, and Eastern Mediterranean regions. Enhanced case-finding activities are expected to increase the number of reported cases. In some countries, the number of cases exceeds the usual background rates of severe acute hepatitis of unknown cause in children. Notably, recent cases have tested negative for the five hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D, and E) that typically account for most hepatitis cases worldwide. Investigations into potential infectious (bacterial, fungal, parasitic, and viral) and non-infectious causes (toxins, medications, autoimmune disorders, and metabolic conditions) are ongoing, but no clear risk factors or causes have been identified to date. The WHO case definition for probable cases includes individuals aged 16 years or younger presenting with acute hepatitis (non-hepatitis A–E) and serum transaminase levels exceeding 500 IU/L (AST or ALT) since October 2021. Cases with other explanations for their clinical presentation are excluded. Testing should prioritize ruling out viral hepatitis A, B, C, and E, as well as assessing the severity of hepatitis through AST/ALT levels.g., Wilson’s disease), or autoimmune disorders. Early consultation with a pediatric hepatologist is recommended to guide the diagnostic workup. Specimen collection should occur as soon as possible after symptom onset and may include multiple specimens over time to support investigations. Specimens should be stored appropriately for future testing and investigations, with ethical considerations and informed consent taken into account for research purposes. Specimens may be referred to national, regional, or global laboratories if local testing capacity is unavailable. Proper storage and transport conditions are outlined for various specimen types, including whole blood, serum, plasma, respiratory specimens, stool, urine, and liver tissue. Investigative diagnostics may involve comprehensive screening for viral and non-viral infections, toxicology, and advanced techniques such as metagenomics to identify potential causes. Metagenomics involves sequencing and analyzing all genetic material in a specimen to detect both known and unknown pathogens. Findings from metagenomics should be confirmed using other laboratory techniques, such as PCR or whole genome sequencing. Data collection should include details on specimen type, collection timing, symptom onset, and treatments received. Laboratories are advised to follow national reporting requirements and share genetic sequence data through publicly accessible databases. WHO encourages member states to identify, investigate, and report potential cases of severe acute hepatitis of unknown cause in children. Access to reliable testing, either locally or through international laboratories, is essential for surveillance. WHO can assist member states in accessing testing and metagenomic analysis internationally if needed. Material transfer agreements may be required for international specimen referral. This interim guidance was developed by the WHO steering group for laboratory and diagnostic stakeholders and will be updated as new information becomes available. It is intended to expire one year after publication unless revised.
